sections.overview: Apamea zeta is a noctuid moth of rocky European mountain grasslands; modern accounts distinguish it from northern forms once included under the same name.
sections.identification: Its variable grey-green to olive forewings bear a pale kidney mark and scalloped lines; the European wingspan is about 41–50 mm.
sections.habitat: It occupies rocky, grass-covered slopes, usually at 1,500–3,000 m, in the Alps and other southern European mountain ranges.
sections.diet: Caterpillars feed on grasses, including tufted hair-grass (Deschampsia cespitosa) in European field observations. Western North American records also name fescues, but those hosts may not represent every population.
sections.behavior: European adults fly from mid-June to late August; larvae shelter in silken cases at grass-tussock bases.
sections.reproduction: Larvae usually overwinter twice, mature before the second winter, and pupate soon after spring returns.
sections.ecology: Close relatives A. maillardi and A. michielii can resemble it; difficult specimens may need genital examination for reliable identification.
sections.conservation: The sources consulted do not establish a global conservation category for the species. A French regional biodiversity database labels it Near Threatened in Nouvelle-Aquitaine; that regional assessment should not be generalized to the entire European range.
